grisly.e: From Middle English grisely, grysly, grissliȝ, griselich, grislich, from Old English grisliċ (“grisly, horrible; dreadful, horrid”), from grīsan (“to shudder with horror.
grisly.x: The photographs of the killings depict a grisly scene.

gristle.e: From Middle English gristel, grystyl, from Old English gristel (“gristle, cartilage”), Proto-West Germanic *gristl, of obscure origin.

groat.e: From Middle English grot, from Old English grot, from Proto-West Germanic *grot, from Proto-Germanic *grutą, related to *greutą. More at grit, grout.

grocer.e: From Old French grossier (“wholesaler”). Compare gross.
grocer.x: “Cadiz isn't going to become the garbage dump capital of the world,” said Patrick Erbacher, a grocer who is vice president of the Cadiz Jaycees.

groggy.x: The medicine made him groggy and irritable.

groin.x: He got kicked in the groin and was writhing in pain.

grommet.e: From obsolete French gromette (“curb chain”) (modern spelling gourmette).

groove.x: The gregarious trifling of life in the social groove.

grope.e: From Middle English gropien, from Old English grāpian, related to grīpan (whence English gripe); compare also grip.
grope.x: That old man groped that girl on the train!

groschen.e: From German Groschen, from Middle High German grosse, from Medieval Latin (denarius) grossus (“thick (penny)”).

grosz.e: Unadapted borrowing from Polish grosz. Doublet of kurus.

grotto.e: From Italian grotta, from Vulgar Latin grupta, from Classical Latin crypta. Doublet of crypt. The Philippine sense is from the holy cave in Lourdes, France.

grouchy.e: US 1895. From grouch + -y. Originally US college student slang.
grouchy.x: His boss gets grouchy when deadlines draw near.

groundbreaking.e: From ground + breaking, in reference to the practice of breaking ground at the beginning of a new building or construction.
groundbreaking.x: The latest model includes several groundbreaking features and improvements.

groundless.e: From Middle English groundles (“bottomless”), from Old English grundlēas, from Proto-Germanic *grundulausaz, equivalent to ground + -less.

groundwater.x: Research has shown bone apatite to undergo chemical exchange with carbonates in either vadose water or groundwater.

groundwork.x: The discovery of the laws of electricity laid the groundwork for a century of innovation.

grouse.e: Attested in the 1530s, as grows ("moorhen"), a plural used collectively. The origin of the noun is unknown.

grove.e: From Middle English grove, grave, from Old English grāf, grāfa (“grove.

grovel.e: From Middle English *grovelen, from Old Norse grufla, grœfla (“to grovel”), from Proto-Germanic *grubilōną (“to dig, delve into”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ‑ (“to…
grovel.x: He had to grovel before his boss after missing the important meeting.

growl.e: From Middle English groulen, grollen, gurlen (“of the bowels: to growl, rumble”), either possibly from Old French groler (variant of croler (“to be agitated, shake”))…
growl.x: A deep growl was the answer I received, and the bear, for such it was, walked quickly away in the same direction whence he had come.

growth.e: From grow + -th (abstract nominal suffix). Compare Old Frisian grēd ("meadow, pasture".
growth.x: Nanoelectronics is one of the area's few growth industries .

grubby.x: He's a grubby little boy, always playing around by the stream.

grudge.x: I have never mentioned it to a human creature; I have kept my grudge to myself. I daresay I have been wicked, but my grudge has grown old with me.

gruel.e: From Middle English gruel, gruwel, greuel, growel (“meal or flour made from beans, lentils, etc.”), from Old French gruel (“coarse meal.

gruelling.e: From present participle of gruel (“to exhaust, punish”), from gruel (noun).

gruesome.e: From grue (“(archaic except Northern England, Scotland) to be frightened.
gruesome.x: The team was so unprepared that the way it played was just gruesome.

gruff.e: 16th century, from Dutch grof and/or Middle Low German grof (both “rough, coarse, rude”), from Old Dutch *grof or Old Saxon *grof, both from Proto-West Germanic *grob…

grumble.e: Probably from Middle French grommeler, from Old French grumeler (“to murmur, grumble”), from Middle Dutch *grommelen ("to murmur, mutter, grunt".
grumble.x: That whiner is never without a grumble to share.

grumpy.x: The old man was grumpy because he couldn’t find his glasses.

grunt.x: The stranger, with a comfortable kind of grunt over his pipe, put his legs up on the settle that he had to himself.

guacamole.e: Borrowed from Spanish guacamole, from Classical Nahuatl āhuacamōlli (from āhuacatl (“avocado”) + mōlli (“sauce; broth”)).

guano.x: In the second experiment, a comparative trial was made between guano and bone-dust mixed with coal ashes.

gudgeon.e: The noun is derived from Late Middle English gojoun [and other forms], from Old French gojon, goujon (“gudgeon”), from Late Latin gōbiōnem, the accusative of gōbiō, the…
gudgeon.x: You save your souls here, eating cabbage, and think you are the righteous. You eat a gudgeon a day, and you think you bribe God with gudgeon.

guerrilla.x: The right-wing paramilitary's offensive against the Marxist guerrillas failed because they did not know the terrain well enough.

guesswork.e: From guess + work. Compare Dutch giswerk (“guesswork”).

guesthouse.e: From Middle English gest hous, gistenehus, gystehuse, gesthus, partly from Old English gæsthūs, ġesthūs (“guesthouse, hostel.

guideline.x: He considered the Ten Commandments more as a guideline than a requirement.

guild.e: From Middle English gilde, from Old Norse gildi (“payment, guild”). Related to geld, yield, yauld.

guile.x: Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and saith of him, Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!

guillemet.e: From French guillemet, diminutive form of the name Guillaume (“William”), named after French typecutter Guillaume Le Bé (1525–1598) who supposedly invented the marks.
guillemet.x: Guillemets, however, proved popular and remain the key method of indicating quotations in French, Arabic, Italian, Greek and many other languages.

guillotine.e: Borrowed from French guillotine, named after the French physician Joseph-Ignace Guillotin (1738–1814), who proposed its use for capital punishment.

gulag.e: Borrowed from Russian ГУЛА́Г (GULÁG), the acronym of Гла́вное управле́ние исправи́тельно-трудовы́х лагере́й (Glávnoje upravlénije ispravítelʹno-trudovýx lageréj, “Chief…

gullet.e: From Middle English golet, borrowed from Old French goulet, from Latin gula.

gullibility.x: What distinguishes the core of the rightwing populist electorate is its gullibility to idiocy-promoting rhetoric against climate science.

gullible.e: Origin uncertain. Either from gull (“to dupe, trick, fool”) + -ible.
gullible.x: Andrew is so gullible, the way he still believes in Santa Claus, the Easter Bunny, the Tooth Fairy, and the Sandman at the age of fourteen.

gully.e: Origin uncertain. Possibly from a variant of Middle English golet (“esophagus, gullet”), from Old French goulet, from Latin gula (“throat”).

gumption.e: Borrowed from Scots gumption (“common sense, shrewdness; drive, initiative”).
gumption.x: Gumption, or rum gumption, docility, comprehenſion, capacity.

gunboat.x: Knock knock. It's the United States. With huge boats (with guns); gunboats.

gunner.e: From Middle English gonner; equivalent to gun + -er.

gunpowder.e: Possibly due to its smell resembling gunpowder during the British Raj.
gunpowder.x: In fact, I’ve long suspected that the popularity of gunpowder or molagapodi outside South India has little to do with the burst of flavours it serves.

gunslinger.x: HIP YOUNG GUNSLINGERS WANTED (BASS, DRUMS, GUITAR) FOR NEW BAND. MUST BE INTO REM, PRIMAL SCREAM, FANCLUB ETC. CONTACT BARRY IN THE SHOP.

gurgle.e: Back formation from Middle English gurguling (“a rumbling in the belly”).
gurgle.x: The bath water gurgled down the drain.

gurney.e: Unknown. Possibly from Gurney cab, a type of horse-drawn cab on wheels named after Theodore Gurney, the US inventor credited with creating and patenting it in about 1883.
gurney.x: The death row convict was strapped into the gurney in order to be given the lethal injection.

gusset.e: From Middle English gusset, gysset, from Old French gosset, gousset (“the hollow of the armpit”), diminutive of gose, gosse (“bean pod, hull, husk”).

guttural.e: From Middle French guttural, from New Latin gutturālis, from Latin guttur (“throat”) + -ālis.
guttural.x: Arabic is considered a very guttural language, with many harsh consonants.

gymnasium.e: From Latin gymnasium, from Ancient Greek γυμνάσιον (gumnásion, “exercise, school”), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”), because Greek athletes trained naked.

gymnast.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek γυμναστής (gumnastḗs, “trainer of athletes”), from γυμνάζω (gumnázō, “I train naked, exercise”), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”).

gymnastic.e: Borrowed from Latin gymnasticus. By surface analysis, gymnast + -ic.

gymnastics.e: From gymnastic: see -ics; from Latin gymnasticus, from Ancient Greek γυμναστικός (gumnastikós), from γυμναστής (gumnastḗs, “athlete, gymnast”), from γῠμνᾰ́ζω (gŭmnắzō…
gymnastics.x: Gymnastics was a significant part of the physical education curriculum.

gynecology.e: From French gynécologie, from Ancient Greek γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”, stem γυναικ-) + -logie (“-logy”). Replaced earlier gyniatrics. By surface analysis, gyneco- + -logy.

gypsum.e: From Latin gypsum, from Ancient Greek γύψος (gúpsos). Doublet of gesso.
gypsum.x: ...but he has been able to analyze the matter removed, and to prove it, by chemical evidence, to consist of Prussian blue, and gypsum principally.

gyrus.e: From Latin gȳrus (“circle”), from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros). Doublet of gyro and gyre.
